questions.q: Without BEGIN/END, how many statements does IF control?
options: Exactly one — the single statement immediately following it
All statements until the next blank line
All statements until the end of the script
It depends on indentation
questions.explain: This is a hard T-SQL rule, regardless of how the code is indented or formatted.

questions.q: Does indentation determine which statements belong to an IF block in T-SQL?
options: No — T-SQL doesn't care about indentation at all; only BEGIN/END actually groups statements
Yes, indented statements are automatically included
Only in stored procedures
Only when using tabs, not spaces
questions.explain: This is a genuinely common beginner trap — code can look correct while behaving completely differently.

options: Wraps any number of statements into one block, treated as a single unit by IF, ELSE, and WHILE
Declares a new variable
Starts and ends a transaction
Creates a stored procedure
questions.explain: BEGIN/END is the actual grouping mechanism T-SQL uses for control-flow blocks.

questions.q: Why does this course wrap even single-statement IF branches in BEGIN/END?
options: It's defensive — if someone later adds a second statement to that branch, the block already behaves correctly
BEGIN/END is required syntax for every IF statement, with no exceptions
It makes the code run faster
It's purely a stylistic choice with no practical benefit

questions.q: In the broken example (IF without BEGIN/END, followed by two statements), which statement actually runs when the IF condition is false?
options: Only the SELECT statement — it runs regardless of the IF condition, since it's not actually part of the IF block
Neither statement runs
Both statements run only when the condition is true
Both statements are skipped entirely
questions.explain: The PRINT is the only statement IF actually controls; the SELECT always executes because it's outside IF's single-statement scope.
